thread.title: Dexcom And The Missing Connection Between Stock Price And Fundamental Business - DexCom, Inc. (NASDAQ:DXCM)

author: Daniel Schönberger
title: Dexcom And The Missing Connection Between Stock Price And Fundamental Business - DexCom, Inc. (NASDAQ:DXCM)
text:
Investing is certainly no easy task. In order to be successful, you have to compete against other investors and you have to consider a lot of different aspects in your (investing) thought process. Fundamental, long-term investing is a lot about assessing the growth potential of a company, looking at the underlying business, its balance sheet and cash flow statement. But successful investing always needs a second, equally important aspect – comparing the current stock price to the intrinsic value. Investing mostly gets interesting because individual people are involved in the decision-making process (buying or selling a stock) and therefore investing is exiting for anyone who is interested in psychology and human behavior.
In the following article, I will analyze a company I have already written about before – the medical device company Dexcom (Nasdaq: DXCM ). I chose the company because it is a great example to show the divergence between fundamental analysis and investing on the one hand and the hype-driven focus on the stock price on the other hand. It is also a great example to show what happens when people forget the connection between fundamental business and stock price. To show that, the article will be divided in three sections: First of all, we will look at the reasons leading to a hype in a certain stock and show why Dexcom is fulfilling these criteria. In a second step, we demonstrate why the stock price is driven by completely unrealistic expectations that lead to false conclusions. Finally, we will finish our article by calculating the intrinsic value of Dexcom again and show why it is extremely overvalued.
DXCM data by YCharts Hype And Overvaluation Although it is extremely difficult to predict the stock market, phases of extreme overvaluation are not just happening randomly. While we can’t predict for a certain stock if such a hype will happen, we can name a few criteria that will support phases of irrational exuberance and function like a fertile soil for a hype. We need a new technology or some kind of technical revolution, we need a potentially gigantic market with difficulties to calculate the exact number and good news about the company supporting the ongoing hype.
New technology leads to hype
In most cases, the starting point for every hype is some kind of new technology, invention or technical revolution. A company is providing a solution for a problem that couldn’t be solved before. Or a company is providing a much more elegant, cheaper or effective way to solve a problem or meet a specific need many people have.
The CGM system Dexcom is providing, certainly has the potential to be a game changer in the treatment of diabetes. The diabetics don’t have to measure the glucose levels by themselves, but the CGM system is providing an updated blood sugar level every five minutes and will inform the diabetic when the blood sugar level is too high, too low or if it is falling or rising very fast.
Potential gigantic market, but problems to measure
A second important “ingredient” is the existence of a potential gigantic market with millions of customers and the possibility to generate extreme amounts of revenue. If investors are pretty confident that only a handful of people will need or use the new technology, we won’t see any kind of hype – despite a potential revolutionary technology. Aside from a big potential market, investors need to have troubles measuring the market accurately. A market with millions of potential customers alone is not enough because only a high level of uncertainty about the actual amounts of future revenue will lead to wild fantasies and completely unrealistic valuations.
In case of Dexcom we have about 30 million diabetics in the United States alone and therefore the potential of a huge customer base. But it is hard to estimate how much of the total number of diabetics will actually use a CGM system.
Good news lead to even higher expectations
But even a potential gigantic market is not enough to lead to a real hype. We also need good news that confirm the wild fantasies and expectations. A string of good news will push expectations as well as the stock price higher and higher. This happens as investors are missing the fact, that the high stock price is already reflecting the good news and the new stories are only confirming what investors expected months or years ago. Investors not only have to look at the fundamental aspects of the company, but always have to compare fundamental data to the current stock price and decide if new pieces of information or new stories will change anything.
In the last few months, there were many different good news for Dexcom that probably led to increasing expectations. For example, in the last four quarters , revenue grew between 24% and 30% in every single quarter (compared to the same quarter last year). But Dexcom could also beat revenue as well as EPS estimates every single time and also raised its guidance last quarter. In March 2018 , Dexcom received FDA approval for the G6 integrated continuous glucose monitoring system: “This is the first CGM product approved for us with other compatible medical devices such as automated insulin dosing systems, insulin pumps, blood glucose meters or other electronic devices used for the management of diabetes.” And finally, in June 2018 , Dexcom announced that the company has received CE Mark for its Dexcom G6 System for people with diabetes that are older than two years. It is understandable, that investors get excited by a company that is growing at about 30% and has the only FDA approved product. But while one can get excited for the fundamental business of the company, you shouldn’t get excited for the stock at current price levels.
Stock price vs. Fundamental Business When criticizing the astronomical valuation of a certain stock and telling people there is no reason to get excited or invest because the stock price doesn’t reflect the fundamental value of a company any more, one usually gets the same counter-arguments presented by the bulls. No matter what stock, no matter what business – the arguments are usually the same.
1. The idea and the new product is revolutionary and it will be a total game changer.
And it certainly is true, that the continuous glucose monitoring system is a great invention with the potential to make the lives of diabetics easier and might also increase the lifespan of diabetics as well as preventing after-effects like problems with feet or problems with eyes.
2. The product meets a market with great potential and several millions of customers while currently only a small fraction of these potential customers are actual customers.
And it is also true, that the market potential is gigantic. With more than 400 million diabetics in the world, we have a very long list of potential customers for Dexcom.
Both of these arguments are true for Dexcom. I would not deny that Dexcom has a great (maybe revolutionary) invention which is meeting a huge market of potential customers. However, we have to look a little closer before we start calculating with billions of dollars in annual revenue. We have to look at the competitors and other products on the market as well as the potential market itself. Let’s start with a closer look at how many diabetics might actually use a CGM system.
The Market
First of all, we have to understand that there are two different main types of diabetes . On the one hand, we have type-1 diabetics with a non-functioning pancreas. They constantly need insulin for their entire life and they also have to monitor their blood sugar levels in order to know if they need to eat something as the blood sugar is too low or have to administer insulin as the blood sugar is too high. On the other hand, we have type-2 diabetics with a pancreas that is working partially, but whose full functionality can be restored. They need insulin only sometimes but are mostly dependent on other drugs. For them, it is also not necessary to constantly monitor the blood sugar levels. We can estimate, that about 5% of all diabetics are type-1 diabetics and about 95% have type-2 diabetes. The main target group for continuous glucose monitoring systems however are type-1 diabetics and only in rare cases type-2 diabetics. This would leave us with about 20 million potential type-1 diabetes patients.
A next important aspect to consider is the fact, where these diabetics live. Not everybody of the 20 million diabetics lives in a country that is rich enough to afford paying for continuous glucose monitoring systems. Even in countries with a high gross domestic product , either insurance has to cover the costs or otherwise only a part of the population can afford buying a continuous glucose monitoring system for themselves (we are talking about amounts between $2,000 and $4,000 annually).
And aside from the financial aspect and the important differentiation between type-1 and type-2 diabetes, we have to consider a third aspect – humans and human behavior . Not everybody might want to pay for it, despite the fact that they could. Human behavior is sometimes interesting and sometimes funny. We just have to accept the fact, that some people don’t care about their personal well-being so much. Some people don’t even accept they have to invest personal time in order to live with the disease and in order to avoid bigger problems in the future. This is a large group we have to keep in mind when thinking about the potential market.
The Competitors
And even after a realistic calculation what the market might be, we can’t assume that people are only buying Dexcom products. In my opinion, Dexcom currently has the best continuous glucose monitoring system on the market, but of course there are other products available that offer incentives for choosing those instead of Dexcom. For example, the product Abbott Laboratories (NYSE: ABT ) is offering (FreeStyle Libre) is similar to Dexcom’s continuous glucose monitoring system although it is not the same technolgoy but has the huge advantage of being much cheaper than the Dexcom product.
A second important point to consider: research doesn’t stop here and now. And when we consider for how long Dexcom has to grow its revenue with extremely high growth rates, we have to assume Dexcom will be market leader at least for two decades. But who can guarantee, that in a few years from now, another company is not offering a cheaper and better product. Who can guarantee another company is not going to introduce the next big innovation making CGM systems obsolete. Apple (Nasdaq: AAPL ) for example is obviously doing research on non-invasive CGM systems, which would be a big leap forward compared to Dexcom’s CGM systems that still require a needle. Although it is unlikely, we also have to think about the possibility of researchers finding a cure for diabetes.
Intrinsic Value Calculation When looking at simple valuation metrics like the price-earnings-ratio (which can’t be calculated as Dexcom is not profitable yet), a price-sales-ratio over 10 and price-cash-flow-ratio over 100 we get a feeling how much Dexcom has to grow in the next decades to justify the current stock price.
Of the potential 20 million customers (type-1 diabetics worldwide) not more than 10 million people live in a country that is rich enough to afford such medical equipment (at most) and let’s say 70% of these 10 million care enough about their health to use and buy a CGM system. This will lead to 7 million potential CGM customers. Following that, we have to think about the market share for Dexcom. What is realistic? Dexcom will certainly not have a market share of 100% but is it rather realistic to assume 50% or 20% over the long term. I think a market share of 50% over the long-term is a very optimistic calculation because Dexcom has to fend off competitors and we have to be sure no other company will introduce an even better CGM system (for example Apple is a potential threat as the tech company might introduce a non-invasive CGM system).
A 50% market share leads to about 3.5 million customers who might spend about $4,000 annually – leading to $14 billion in annual revenue for Dexcom. In my last article I already provided a calculation assuming an annual revenue of $16 billion in 20 years. The intrinsic value in such a scenario would be $111 making Dexcom almost fairly valued.
(Source: Own Work, originally published here )
And even in that scenario where Dexcom is fairly valued right now, we have to consider that this is an unrealistic scenario. We assume a high market share and an extremely high number of type-1 diabetics using CGM systems - which is just unrealistic. And it is dangerous for investors to calculate with unrealistic, overly optimistic scenarios.
Conclusion I am not advising to short Dexcom. I am also not saying that you can’t buy Dexcom and maybe profit from short-term gains as the stock might go higher in the next few months. But Dexcom is definitely no long-term investment although we are talking about a great company with long-term growth potential. The company however has to grow at rates that almost seem impossible (or at least unrealistic) and it also has to grow for a very long time in order to justify the current price. The most important lesson is to compare the fundamental business and the calculated intrinsic value with the actual stock price. Only because we are talking about a high-growth company doesn’t mean it is a great investment.
